blocks.md: Least squares can be pictured as dropping a perpendicular. The outcome is a point in space, and all the predictions the regressors could possibly make form a flat surface. The fitted values are the point on that surface closest to the outcome, and the residuals are the perpendicular gap between them. Two matrices do this job: one projects any outcome onto the surface to give fitted values, the other produces what is left over.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: This geometry explains why residuals are uncorrelated with every regressor, where degrees of freedom come from, and how controlling for variables works.
The geometry behind [OLS in Matrix Form](note:ols-in-matrix-form). Two matrices do all the work.

- $\mathbf{P}$ is the **projection (hat) matrix**: $\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{P}\mathbf{y}$ is the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{y}$ onto the column space of $\mathbf{X}$.
- $\mathbf{M}$ is the **residual maker**: $\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{M}\mathbf{y}$.

| Property | Statement | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Decomposition | $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{P}\mathbf{y} + \mathbf{M}\mathbf{y}$ | Fit plus residual, and the pieces are orthogonal |
| Symmetry | $\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{P}'$, $\mathbf{M} = \mathbf{M}'$ | Needed in variance derivations |
| Idempotency | $\mathbf{P}\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{P}$, $\mathbf{M}\mathbf{M} = \mathbf{M}$ | Projecting twice changes nothing — the geometric content |
| Annihilation | $\mathbf{M}\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{0}$ | **Fundamental.** Regressing a column of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{X}$ gives a perfect fit and zero residuals |
| Orthogonality | $\mathbf{P}\mathbf{M} = \mathbf{M}\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{0}$ | Fitted space and residual space are orthogonal complements |
| Singularity | $\mathbf{M}^{-1}$ does not exist | $\mathbf{M}$ has rank $n-K$, not $n$ |
| Traces | $\mathrm{trace}(\mathbf{P}) = K$, $\mathrm{trace}(\mathbf{M}) = n-K$ | This is where the degrees of freedom come from |

**Symmetry**: $\mathbf{M}' = \mathbf{I} - [\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}']' = \mathbf{I} - \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}' = \mathbf{M}$, using that $(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}$ is symmetric.

**Idempotency**: $\mathbf{P}\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}' = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}' = \mathbf{P}$. Then $\mathbf{M}\mathbf{M} = \mathbf{I} - 2\mathbf{P} + \mathbf{P}\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{I} - \mathbf{P} = \mathbf{M}$.
**Annihilation**: $\mathbf{M}\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{X} - \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{X} - \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{0}$.

sections.heading: Why MX = 0 is the fundamental result

blocks.md: It gives

The OLS residual vector is the projection of the **disturbances** onto the orthogonal complement of $\mathbf{X}$'s column space. That single line is the source of $E[\mathbf{e}'\mathbf{e}] = (n-K)\sigma^2$ and hence the unbiasedness of $\widehat{\sigma}^2$ — see [Sampling Distribution of OLS](note:sampling-distribution-of-ols).

sections.heading: Trace, rank and degrees of freedom

blocks.md: $\mathbf{M}$ is idempotent and symmetric, so its rank equals its trace:
using the cyclic property of the [Trace of a Matrix](note:trace-of-a-matrix). Then

$h_i$, the $i$-th diagonal element of $\mathbf{P}$, is the **leverage** of observation $i$ — how far $\mathbf{x}_i$ sits from the centre of the design space. Since $\mathrm{trace}(\mathbf{P}) = K$, the leverages sum to $K$ and average $K/n$. That is where the $2K/n$ cut-off in [Regression Diagnostics](note:regression-diagnostics) comes from (written there as $2p/n$, with $p = K$ parameters).

sections.heading: Results when X contains a constant

blocks.md: With $\mathbf{X} = [\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{x}_2, \dots, \mathbf{x}_K]$ and $\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{0}$, the first column gives $\mathbf{1}'\mathbf{e} = 0$ — residuals sum to zero. And
The regression line passes through the means. Neither holds without a constant.
The simplest projection, and the building block of the general one. Projecting $\mathbf{b}$ onto the line through $\mathbf{a}$:

Example: $\mathbf{a} = (1,1)'$, $\mathbf{b} = (3,1)'$ gives $\mathbf{p} = (2,2)'$ and residual $(1,-1)'$, which is orthogonal to $\mathbf{a}$ ([Inner Products and Orthogonality](note:inner-products-and-orthogonality)).
Two special cases worth knowing:

- **Regression through the origin**: the slope is $\mathbf{a}'\mathbf{b}/\mathbf{a}'\mathbf{a}$ — this formula with $\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{x}$.
- **Regression on a constant**: with $\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{1}$, $\mathbf{p} = \bar{y}\,\mathbf{1}$. The projection onto the constant is the mean, and $\mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{1}}\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{y} - \bar{y}\mathbf{1}$ is the demeaned variable. Demeaning *is* partialling out a constant.
The general $\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'$ does the same thing onto the whole [Column Space](note:column-space) of $\mathbf{X}$.
